data.title: Trump, Cotton tussle over daylight savings after cell phone number leak
data.description:
President Trump repeatedly berated Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) on Saturday over his stance on a daylight savings bill after posting the Republican Congress member’s cell phone number on social media. 

In a morning Truth Social post, the president encouraged his supporters to call the senator and urge him to back legislation that would make daylight savings time the permanent standard time. After Cotton stood by his position in a brief statement shared later Saturday, which didn’t directly mention the president or the leak, Trump went back on the offensive.

“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” Cotton’s post read. “Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first.”

Trump responded on Truth Social, “If Tom Cotton were putting Arkansas first, he would give them an extra hour of daylight and, more importantly, they wouldn’t have to run all over their houses, farms, work places, and everywhere else, twice a year, having to change their Clocks, and often forgetting to do so.”

“That is really putting Arkansas FIRST, and I know, because, unlike Tom, I won that Great State, three times, and by almost 40 points!” the president continued.

The president has repeatedly pushed Congress to pass the Sunshine Protection Act of 2025, claiming in his post that the move would decrease the national crime rate because “CRIMINALS DON’T LIKE WORKING IN THE LIGHT.”

In his first post targeting Cotton, Trump blamed the GOP lawmaker for holding up the bill in the Senate after the House passed the legislation in July with broad bipartisan support. 

“To the Great People of Arkansas, please let your Senator know it would be a GREAT Bipartisan WIN for the United States Senate, and for America, itself. Call Tom on his cellphone,” the president wrote before sharing Cotton’s number. “Let him know.” 

In one of two follow-up post on Saturday afternoon, the president pushed back on the senator’s resistance to changing his position on this bill and called Cotton’s stance “ego” driven.

Trump wrote in his other post that “a table full of very distinguished people” told him “they HATE” going home at night in the dark after the daylight savings time change. 

“It’s depressing! One of the gentleman stated that, ‘I just hate going home in darkness,’” the president wrote. “It’s also, in Crime Ridden Blue States, a lot more dangerous to be walking home in the dark!”

As of 3:30 p.m. on Saturday, Cotton has not responded to Trump’s second and third Truth Social posts against him. The Hill has reached out to the Arkansas senator for comment.

data.title: White House defends media outlet bans, now citing 'professionalism' standards
data.description:
Trump administration lawyers are fighting back against CNN, MS NOW and Politico’s attempt to prevent the White House from enforcing futures bans against them — with the Justice Department (DOJ) now arguing the three outlets failed to meet “professional” standards.

“The President concluded that they have failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including’ by ‘publishing sensitive or classified information,’” the DOJ attorneys representing President Trump wrote in a Friday night court filing. 

The filing comes as Trump continues his efforts to restrict these networks’ coverage of him despite a federal judge ruling against a previous White House grounds ban. Most recently, the administration prevented CNN from fulfilling two previously scheduled television press pool duties, barring its reporters from traveling with the president.

The Friday filing cites Truth Social posts from the president in the days following the ban, where Trump wrote that “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press,” but rather “instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS.”

The DOJ legal team reupped its claims that CNN, MS NOW and Politico jeopardized national security by “publishing classified” information, with the department now adding they believe their reporting on the administration demonstrates these networks “have failed to maintain minimum professional journalistic standards.”

The filing also argued that, throughout history, presidents have “have long decided which journalists should receive privileged access, which has varied substantially from administration to administration” — including George Washington handpicking journalists “based on political considerations” for his Farewell Address.

Trump initially banned the outlets in September, with TV “pool,” as it is known — consisting of CNN, Fox News, ABC, NBC and CBS — issuing a statement blasting the president’s move to keep CNN from the White House. The group then held back coverage of the president for days in solidarity with the cable channel.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that the White House violated the media companies’ due process rights, and access for journalists working for the three outlets was restored.

The DOJ has sought to reinstate the ban, with senior counsel Michael Velchik writing in a past court filing, “After all, access to the White House is a privilege — not a right.”

Attorney General Todd Blanche also said on Sunday that “the president hasn’t denied access” to the outlets.

“That’s not the right way to describe it. This is what the president has said –– is that he is sick and tired of certain media outlets just refusing to report accurate news,” he said. 

The Trump administration now faces a new fight over the White House preventing CNN reporters from fulfilling their press pool duties for his trip to Knoxville for Tennessee-Texas college football game, as well as campaign events in Oklahoma and Texas.

data.title: The next crash could be an economic bloodbath
data.description:
We have moved well past the point where artificial intelligence represents a simple software upgrade or a clever chat interface on a smartphone. The sheer magnitude of capital flowing into digital infrastructure has transformed a speculative tech trend into a foundational pillar of the global economy. This is concerning on many levels.

Capital expenditure figures for big tech firms look less like corporate budgets and more like the defense spending of major nation-states. Trillions of dollars are surging directly into silicon chips, liquid-cooled data centers, concrete foundations, nuclear power restarts, and high-voltage power grids. Heavy industry, commercial real estate, utility providers, and green energy developers have all tied their long-term growth forecasts to an endless appetite for computer power.

Silicon Valley has successfully exported its financial risk to the real world. If investors suddenly conclude that these massive physical assets will never generate meaningful returns, the economic shockwave could reach cement factories and power plants long before it reaches California’s office parks.

At the heart of this vulnerability lies a mountain of speculative math. Tech giants and venture capital firms are pouring billions into infrastructure to meet software demand that, for now, exists mostly in pitch decks.

Constructing a modern data center requires hundreds of millions of dollars upfront, backed by decades-long power contracts and short-lived hardware assets that depreciate faster than luxury sports cars.

Nvidia GPUs can depreciate rapidly when faster chips hit the market. If enterprise software revenue lands at a tiny fraction of current forecasts, those sparkling new server farms could become vast monuments to overinvestment. Valuations built on exponential growth projections could evaporate overnight, leaving corporations with warehouses full of costly hardware that is already becoming obsolete.

Ordinary citizens who avoid tech news entirely remain heavily exposed to the risks of this potential time bomb. The modern stock market has grown historically top-heavy, with a tiny handful of mega-cap technology firms driving the vast majority of broad index returns. Pension funds, state retirement systems, index-tracking mutual funds, and standard 401(k) accounts have spent years automatically purchasing these exact corporate giants.

An office worker in Ohio or a teacher in Texas might not know the difference between an LLM and a GPU, and they might not care, yet their financial security rests directly on tech stock valuations. A sudden correction in a few Silicon Valley boardrooms translates into a direct haircut for everyday retirement portfolios.

The employment market contains an even more twisted paradox. Over the last three years, corporate leaders across finance, logistics and retail justified aggressive hiring freezes, office expansions and massive capital borrowing by promising shareholders that automation would soon drastically lower labor costs. The gravity of this shift is underscored by a senior figure at Microsoft, who says the entire generative AI model relies on “the largest theft of labor in human history.”

Company executives essentially took out heavy loans against future productivity gains that have yet to show up in national economic data. If software fails to automate administrative workloads at scale, those same executives will face immediate margin pressure. The corporate response to missed productivity targets will likely involve rapid, aggressive cost-cutting. Thousands of workers could lose their jobs as companies scramble to offset the staggering costs of unused software subscriptions and useless infrastructure commitments.

The financial system itself adds a dangerous final layer to this setup. Wall Street banks, private equity funds and non-bank lenders have spent years funding data center construction, energy acquisitions and specialized hardware leases. Private credit funds in particular have poured billions into leveraged loans for unproven tech ventures, seeking higher yields in a volatile market. When an asset class backed by heavy leverage suddenly loses its revenue potential, the debt doesn’t simply disappear. Defaulted loans on underused data centers could move from corporate balance sheets into regional banks and private credit markets.

We saw a similar chain reaction when risky housing debt spread losses across financial institutions worldwide. A sudden collapse in hardware valuations would quickly turn software failure into a banking nightmare, complete with liquidity squeezes and frozen credit markets. The financial consensus currently assumes that digital infrastructure represents a bulletproof asset class with zero downside. But history suggests that whenever Wall Street treats speculative future yield as a guaranteed certainty, the bill eventually arrives with substantial interest.

John Mac Ghlionn is a writer and researcher who explores culture, society and the impact of technology on daily life.

data.title: Florida's dengue outbreak reportedly largest US has seen in decades
data.description:
A dengue fever outbreak in the state of Florida appears to have grown to the largest in the continental U.S. in decades, totaling 252 reported cases this year in the Sunshine State according to an update this week.

Dengue fever, which is transmitted through infected mosquito bites, is rarely fatal and most infected people do not experience symptoms. However, it can cause fever, eye and joint pain, nausea and rash, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Last month, Florida reported one death from the virus of an elderly woman in Tampa. 

Hillsborough County had the highest level of reports, with a total of 223 locally-spread cases. Hillsborough encompasses the Tampa area and is the fourth-most populous county in the state.

County officials have declared a state of emergency amid this outbreak, with Hillsborough County Administrator Bonnie Wise extending this order this week amid ongoing efforts to control the local mosquito population. 

The county is encouraging residents to take steps to mitigate the spread of this virus, including draining stagnant water, wearing protective clothing when going outside and using bug spray.

Florida routinely sees some of the highest levels of reported dengue contractions in the continental U.S. The state’s warm weather is conducive for the breed of mosquitos that spreads dengue. In 2023, Florida reported 200 locally-spread cases. 

In the U.S. more broadly, Puerto Rico also sees high levels of dengue. The territory reported 922 of the total 2,145 locally-acquired cases in the country this year, according to the CDC. 

The largest-ever outbreak in the U.S. occurred in Hawaii over a six month period between 2015 and 2016, with a total of 264 locally-acquired cases.

data.title: Breaking the tyranny of extremists
data.description:
The nearly unchecked powers of the president are controlled by the ideologues and special interests who dictate Republican nominations. Self-serving agendas take precedence over the selection of candidates with a record of abiding by the rule of law and the Constitution. Without urgent reforms, America will continue to succumb to what the Framers of the Constitution most feared — a populist tyranny.

Two consequential changes have brought us to this crossroads.

The first: Control over nominations has shifted since the 1970s. Party officials committed to winning general elections with experienced candidates gave way to relatively small and ideologically unrepresentative segments of the electorate intent on advancing their narrow agendas. The relatively low turnout for direct primaries enabled evangelicals, members of the Christian right as well as virulent opponents of immigration, abortion, taxes, and government regulation to control the delegates to national conventions who select presidential candidates.

These changes overturned the Constitution’s design to “filter” the voice of the people and insulate elected officials, especially presidents. The Electoral College, Alexander Hamilton explained in 1788, was designed to produce “a constant probability of seeing the station filled by characters preeminent for ability and virtue” and preventing the selection of presidents inclined toward “cabal, intrigue, and corruption.”

President Trump is the nightmare. He won the 2016 nomination by scraping together less than 40 percent in early primary contests among a crowded field of opponents. As is typical of Republican primaries, three out of four voters identified as very or somewhat conservative and Trump won pluralities there. In contrast, about two-thirds of voters in the 2016 general election described themselves as moderate or liberal.

Trump’s open disregard for the rule of law and the Constitution was not a serious consideration for voters in the Republican primaries and the November general election. Nearly all Republicans robotically backed him in an era of intense party loyalty. A plurality of the remaining voters, including independents, were swayed largely by their reaction against Democrats: dislike of Hillary Clinton, opposition to the Obama administration, economic and cultural dissatisfaction and a desire for political change.

The second momentous change has been the expansion of presidential powers to act unilaterally in domestic and international affairs. Democrats and Republicans left a loaded gun in the Oval Office.

With the onset of the Cold War, presidents routinely acted alone to send troops into real or potential conflicts, conduct assassinations abroad, and reach international agreements. Extreme abuses of power were mostly skirted by the vetting of political parties and their networks. They weeded out demagogues from the pool of presidential candidates and nominated, in most cases, candidates with a track record for governing effectively.

Then came Trump — a candidate propelled to the cusp of election by narrow ideological factions without the peer review of senior elected and party officials who are attentive to the rule of law. The result: imperial power is unmoored at a time that lacks protections against unqualified and unscrupulous presidents.

Saving the republic now requires urgent reforms of the nomination process to filter out the demagogues that most worried the Constitution’s Framers. Changes are needed in both parties but most urgently in the Republican Party that lacks the informal checks from moderate donors and insiders.

A necessary starting point is to restore and expand the independence of unpledged Republican delegates: the national and state GOP leaders focused on protecting the party’s national reputation.

Until 2012, nearly a fifth of convention delegates were free to vote for any presidential candidate on the first ballot regardless of their state’s primary or caucus results. By 2016, the proportion of unpledged delegates was slashed to 6.9 percent and national and state party rules increasingly bound them to primary results.

Urgent reforms to restore balance to the Republican nomination process are possible but must be achieved soon. The party should maintain the central role of primary voters while also returning the ability of party leaders to create an off-ramp if activists favor a candidate who is a threat to rule of law and Constitution.

Ideologues will throw up a predictable smoke screen, claiming that the reforms weaken democracy. The truth is that primary voters will continue to dominate the selection of candidates. But in cases where activists are on the verge of imposing a candidate with extreme views about policy and the rule of law, party leaders must reserve a limited option to leverage their small fraction of delegates to tilt a convention toward alternatives better suited to our constitutional system and the views of most Americans.

Unless immediate and vigorous action is taken, the nomination of another vengeful and unprincipled presidential candidate is a very real possibility in 2028.

Lawrence R. Jacobs is the Walter F. and Joan Mondale Chair for Political Studies and director of the Center for the Study of Politics and Governance at the University of Minnesota’s Humphrey School of Public Affairs. A member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, he has written or edited 19 books on American politics.

data.title: Tennessee corrections commissioner to resign after botched Christa Pike execution
data.description:
The head of Tennessee’s corrections department will step down following the state’s botched execution of death row inmate Christa Pike this week. 

Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada submitted his resignation on Saturday, Gov. Bill Lee (R-Tenn.) announced. 

“Commissioner Strada has served with integrity, and I appreciate his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment,” Lee said in a statement shared by his office. 

“I have accepted his decision to step down and am grateful for his commitment to ensuring a smooth leadership transition,” the governor continued. “I thank Commissioner Strada for his dedicated service to Tennessee and pray God’s blessings over him in the days ahead.”

Strada has served in this role since Lee appointed him as commissioner in 2023. Previously, he was the deputy director at the Arizona Department of Corrections and worked for the Federal Bureau of Prisons for 30 years. 

In a statement shared by the governor’s office, the commissioner called his time overseeing the department “a great honor,” and expressed his support for the independent investigation ordered by Lee into the failed execution attempt.

“I continue to believe the Department carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol,” Strada said. 

“Even so, stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward,” he continued. “I believe this review is entirely appropriate and necessary, and I look forward to doing everything I can to help determine exactly what occurred.”

Lee ordered that Pike’s execution be delayed until at least next year after she survived two lethal injection attempts on Wednesday. Pike’s lawyers said during a Thursday press conference she was receiving “lifesaving care” in the hospital. 

Attorney Randy Spivey, who witnessed the execution attempt, said state executioners “attempted to establish an IV line for an hour,” and used seven needles in Pike’s left arm alone.  

“The state of Tennessee has shown us again that they are not capable of carrying out an execution consistent with basic human dignity,” Spivey said. “Last night was not just inefficient. It was cruel and it was torturous.”

Pike was convicted in the 1995 murder of her 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville, Tenn., with her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp. Shipp was not eligible for the death penalty because he was 17 at the time of the crime and is serving out a life sentence in prison. 

Earlier this year, the governor granted a one-year reprieve for another death row inmate after state executioners failed to locate a vein for a lethal injection in Tony Carruthers. 

Lee said in his Friday statement an interim commissioner would be announced “at a later date.”

data.title: Ted Cruz slams Tucker Carlson for World War II comments
data.description:
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) slammed conservative commentator Tucker Carlson for a recent podcast appearance during which the former Fox News host questioned whether the United Kingdom “benefited” from its involvement in the second World War.

“Yes, Tucker, the UK is better off for winning WWII,” Cruz responded to the clip in a Friday night post to social platform X.

He continued, “America is better off for winning World War II. And the world would be much worse off if the Nazis had won WWII. This is not complicated.”

Carlson’s comments came during his interview with former U.K. conservative lawmaker Jacob Rees-Mogg, where the commentator made several controversial claims about WWII.

In a segment of the interview, called “Was WWII good for Britain?”, Carlson expressed doubt on whether the U.K. “won” after it helped defeat the Axis powers.

“Has the U.K. benefited from it?” Carlson asked. “There are a lot of people in Britain who can’t speak English, so it would be nice to have at least a European language spoken in your country.”

“Why don’t you tell me the ways in which Britain benefited from — I’m going to use quotes here — ‘winning the Second World War.’ Because from my perspective, it looks like the empire ended. India was lost two years later, the United States took over the world, and has had troops here ever since,” he continued.

Since Carlson’s exit from Fox News in 2023, he grown more controversial among Republican lawmakers — notably drawing ire for hosting a Holocaust revisionist on his self-titled show in 2024.

Throughout the episode, podcaster Darryl Cooper made controversial comments about Nazi Germany’s mass murder of Jewish people, claiming the genocide was a result of poor planning.

Carlson also hosted white nationalist commentator Nick Fuentes on his podcast. Fuentes has denied the Holocaust on multiple occasions and made several antisemitic remarks during his discussion with Carlson.  

At the time, Cruz criticized Carlson for interviewing Fuentes, saying at the Republican Jewish Coalition Annual Summit, “If you sit there with someone who says Adolf Hitler was very cool and that their mission is to defeat ‘global Jewry,’ and you say nothing, then you are a coward, and you are complicit in that evil.”

data.title: Nepal's catastrophic flooding is a red alert for the world's mountain towns
data.description:
In 2011, I trekked with scientists and engineers to about 17,000 feet to look at Lake Imja in Nepal’s Everest region. I thought about that expedition from the safety of my home in Peru as I watched the awful consequences of permafrost weakened by warming upon the northern district of Rasuwa, near Nepal’s border with Tibet. 

When glaciers recede, they leave an indent created by their weight. Melt from the glacier fills that bowl, growing until the pressure gets too great, or an earthquake hits. Lake Imja did not exist in 1953, when Sir Edmund Hillary conquered Everest. By 2011, it was the fastest-growing of some 1,600 glacier lakes in Nepal.

On our visit, the artificial lake stretched down from the glacier for a mile and a half, held in place by a precarious mix of debris. An earthquake or pressure on the makeshift dam could release water with disastrous consequences for vulnerable communities in Nepal. 

On Aug. 26, the world watched the consequences of a different version of what we feared. Above Rasuwa, a broken chunk of glacier, likely the size of a big New York City building, fell 4,000 feet, setting off a tsunami. Friction at that velocity melts ice. A great wave gathered ice, snow, water, rocks and mud — and then structures — to cascade down the narrow valleys, wiping out lives, communities and infrastructure. Hurricane-force winds leveled trees. 

I’m safe as I write, but some version of the same can and likely will happen in my country and other mountainous regions, and again in Nepal. Towers of ice and snow weakened by a quickly heating planet will, one way or another, wreak havoc down-mountain in vulnerable landscapes.  

We came back from our Lake Imja expedition shaken, but also with thoughts about how to anticipate and prepare against these disasters.  

Early warning systems with real-time sensors and satellite communications can detect sudden water releases and alert downstream communities. It could help to slowly lower water levels in high-risk glacial lakes and, where possible, to future-proofing buildings and installations. Lake Imja was a slightly different situation than what happened in Rasuwa, but it carries the same danger and is more like the situation in my country.  

In Peru, Palcacocha is a glacial lake in Huaraz Province. The spectacular snow-covered peaks of that part of the Andes mountain range are warming, creating the same conditions as we saw in Nepal. One hundred thousand people live below our lake, including communities and schools that inevitably will be directly in the pathway should meltwater be released and trigger a chain reaction not unlike what happened in Nepal.   

Part of my job as executive director of the Instituto Andino de Montaña in Peru was to persuade the city of Huaraz to put an early warning system in place. After much effort, we achieved that. But when we tried to get officials to commit to engineering to lower the lake’s water level, we encountered red tape, indolence, wrong priorities and fear of scaring away tourists. No funding or commitment was forthcoming.   

Since then, we have been holding our breath and hoping for the best. But with the ongoing El Niño event, this could be the season when our worst fears come about.   

The grassroots Peruvians I work with in the countryside have no trust that government officials will protect them against these well-known risks. Huaraz is very far from Lima, our capital, and the people at risk feel invisible. Officials at the federal level are trying to pass the buck to local and private actors. But no one at the local, provincial or even regional level has the technical capacity to take on this challenging engineering work.  

The U.S., where I got my Ph.D., is not immune. Melting glaciers already trigger disastrous floods and mudslides. A glacial lake outburst flood has occurred every year since 2011 at Suicide Basin, on the Mendenhall Glacier near Juneau, Alaska. The rapid retreat of the Grasshopper Glacier in Wyoming’s Wind River Mountains triggered a glacial lake outburst flood in 2003.

American communities will suffer a quieter, less visible threat — the toxic minerals and metals from melting glaciers that leak into local water supplies, eroding life rather than blasting it away.

If disaster happens anywhere, in my country, or any number of American communities as this threat evolves, there will be official mourning. Why not invest that energy and empathy into acting now and saving lives, rather than grieving them?

Jorge Recharte Bullard Ph.D. has served as president of Instituto Andino de Montaña, the Mountain Institute’s Legacy Institution, since 2020. He was director of the Andean program of The Mountain Institute between 1997 and 2019.

data.title: Trump posts GOP senator's cell phone number over daylight savings act stall
data.description:
President Trump posted Sen. Tom Cotton’s (R-Ark.) cell phone number on Truth Social Saturday, lashing out at Senate Republicans to move forward with legislation that would make daylight saving time permanent.

“Tom Cotton, a friend of mine, is holding up a very important Bill,” Trump wrote, describing the Sunshine Protection Act. “For some reason, Tom is stopping the Bill and, in the Senate, it’s very easy to do, it only takes one! It should pass overwhelmingly, in a Bipartisan fashion.”

“To the Great People of Arkansas, please let your Senator know it would be a GREAT Bipartisan WIN for the United States Senate, and for America, itself. Call Tom on his cellphone,” the president continued before he wrote the number. “Let him know.”

Trump blamed Cotton for the bill — which he called the “No More Changing of Clocks Act” — stalling in the Senate after it passed the House with a 308-117 vote.

Cotton has been among the most vocal opponents of permanent daylight saving time —expressing concern that without the twice a year clock changes, many children heading to school and millions of Americans traveling to work would be left in the dark.

“If permanent daylight saving time becomes the law of the land, it will again make winter a dark and dismal time for millions of Americans,” he said last year.

Trump countered that more evening daylight would help reduce crime and traffic accidents, while benefiting public health and industries including sports, tourism, restaurants and retail.

In his Saturday Truth Social post, Trump continued that the bill would help the PGA Tour who “needs more Daylight in the afternoon in order to finish their Tournaments.”

“Likewise, regular Golfers, Tennis Players, Hunters and, perhaps most importantly, Farmers who want more Daylight to play or work,” he added.

The post included a letter from PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp who wrote in “strong support” of the bill — citing that it would generate $1 billion annually in new direct revenue for the sport. 

Trump has pushed for the Sunshine Protect Act’s passage since August, but Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has cast doubt on whether the measure can secure the 60 votes needed to advance.

Cotton’s office did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.

data.title: Pennsylvania nears 1,000 measles cases, state health department reports
data.description:
Pennsylvania’s reported measles cases are almost at 1,000 for 2026, days after its health department confirmed the figure had passed 900.

“977 measles cases have been confirmed across 39 counties in Pennsylvania so far in 2026,” Pennsylvania’s Department of Health wrote in a statement Friday. 

The agency highlighted that 34 new Pennsylvania measles cases had emerged since Sept. 30, with hospitalizations tied to the infection reaching 195. The statement also reemphasized the state’s reported five measles-associated deaths amid an ongoing dispute between Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. over the outbreak’s true death toll.

The outbreak is the worst the commonwealth has seen in more than 35 years.

Pennsylvania’s Department of Health added Friday that all but four of its measles cases have been among people who were not fully vaccinated against the virus.

“In a typical month, Pennsylvania health care providers administer approximately 25,000 doses of the MMR vaccine,” it wrote. “In August 2026, more than 49,000 MMR vaccines were administered and so far in September 2026, more than 53,000 doses have been administered.”

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) describes measles as a highly contagious virus but adds that two doses of the MMR vaccine provide the best protection. Pennsylvania’s health department stated that both doses together are 97 percent effective at preventing measles for life.

Earlier this month, the Pennsylvania Department of Health began the process of requesting emergency assistance from the CDC’s Epi-Aid program following five reported deaths tied to the infection, but only on the condition that the federal agency publicly recognizes the state’s entire reported death count. 

The CDC has refused to acknowledge the same number of deaths as the Keystone State in its national count, sparking a bitter political dispute between Shapiro and Kennedy over what constitutes a measles death.  

The federal agency to date has only recognized two deaths in its measles cases and outbreaks index, though the website adds that “this number is subject to change.”

The CDC’s database does not specify where or when these deaths occurred, so it’s not clear if the tally includes Pennsylvania’s reported cases. However, no other state has recorded a measles death this year. 

In 2025, three people in the U.S. died from measles — two in Texas and one in New Mexico.
